Probably from Old English hēo (whence dialectal English hoo), with an irregular change in stress from hēo to heō /hjoː/, then a development from /hj-/ to /ç/ to /ʃ-/, similar to the derivation of Shetland from Old Norse Hjaltland.

examples.text: I go to work on foot every day.

translations.fr: Je vais au travail à pied tous les jours.
translations.pt: Eu vou a pé para o trabalho todos os dias.

examples.text: She went to the movies yesterday.

translations.de: Sie ist gestern ins Kino gegangen.
translations.fr: Elle est allée au cinéma hier.
translations.pt: Ela foi ao cinema ontem.

more.definition: To move through space (especially to or through a place). (May be used of tangible things such as people or cars, or intangible things such as moods or information.); To move or travel through time (either literally—in a fictional or hypothetical situation in which time travel is possible—or in one's mind or knowledge of the historical record). (See also go back.); To navigate (to a file or folder on a computer, a site on the internet, a memory, etc.).
collocations: go for a walk — to take a walk
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁-der. From Middle English gon, goon, from Old English gān (“to go”), from Proto-West Germanic *gān, from Proto-Germanic *gāną (“to go”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰeh₁- (“to leave”). The inherited past tense form yode (compare Old English ēode) was replaced through suppletion in the 15th century by went, from Old English wendan (“to go, depart, wend”).

more.definition: Supposing that, assuming that, in the circumstances that; suppositive used to introduce a condition that may be (or prove to be) either true or false.; A keyword that invokes conditional processing: in the event that a given condition is true, execute the given statement(s) (otherwise execute other statements).; Supposing that; used with past or past perfect subjunctive to indicate a counterfactual or hypothetical condition.
more.etymology: From Middle English if, yif, yef, from Old English ġif (“if”), from Proto-West Germanic *jabu, *jabē, from Proto-Germanic *jabai (“when, if”). Cognate with Scots gif (“if, whether”), Saterland Frisian af, of (“if, whether”), West Frisian oft (“whether”), Dutch of (“or, whether, but”), Middle Low German ef, if, af, of ("if; whether"; > German Low German of), German ob (“if, whether”), Icelandic ef (“if”).

more.definition: Designating the side of the body which is positioned to the east if one is facing north, the side on which the heart is not located in most humans. This arrow points to the reader's right: →; Clockwise, particularly when describing a change in direction or orientation.; Complying with justice, correctness, or reason; correct, just, true. See also the interjection senses below.
more.etymology: From Middle English reȝt, right, righte, riht, riȝt, riȝte, ryght, ryȝt, from Old English reht, reoht, rieht, riht, ryht (“right,” also the word for “straight” and “direct”), from Proto-West Germanic *reht, from Proto-Germanic *rehtaz (“right, straight; just, morally upright”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtós (“right, straightened”), from *h₃reǵ- (“to straighten; to righten”).

more.definition: On the right side.; Towards the right side.; Exactly, precisely.
more.etymology: From Middle English right, righte, from Old English rihte, rehte (“right; rightly; due; directly; straight”), from Proto-Germanic *rehta, from *rehtaz (“right; straight”).

more.definition: That which complies with justice, law or reason.; A legal, just or moral entitlement.; The right side or direction.
more.etymology: From Middle English right, from Old English riht, reht, ġeriht (“that which is right, just, or proper”), from Proto-West Germanic *reht, from Proto-Germanic *rehtą (“a right”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵtom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵt- (“to straighten; direct”). Cognate with Dutch recht (“a right; privilege”), German Recht (“a right”), Danish ret (“a right”).

more.definition: Away from the inside or centre.; Away from, or at a distance from, some point of reference or focus.; Specifically, away from home or one's usual place.
more.etymology: From Middle English out, oute, from a combination of Old English ūt (“out”, preposition & adverb), from Proto-West Germanic *ūt, from Proto-Germanic *ūt (“out”); and Old English ūte (“outside; without”, adverb), from Proto-Germanic *ūtai (“out; outside”); both from Proto-Indo-European *úd (“upwards, away”).

more.definition: On all sides, or in every or any direction from a point; around.; Here and there; around; in one place and another; up and down.; From one place or position to another in succession; indicating repeated movement or activity.

Preposition and adverb from Middle English aboute, abouten, from Old English abūtan, onbūtan, from on (“in, on”) + būtan (“outside of”) (compare modern English but, bout), itself from be (“by”) + ūtan (“outside”); equivalent to on + be + out or on + but. Cognate with Old Frisian abûta (“outside; except”).

more.definition: In a circle around; all round; on every side of; on the outside of; around.; Over or upon different parts of; through or over in various directions; here and there in; to and fro in; throughout.; See about to.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Preposition and adverb from Middle English aboute, abouten, from Old English abūtan, onbūtan, from on (“in, on”) + būtan (“outside of”) (compare modern English but, bout), itself from be (“by”) + ūtan (“outside”); equivalent to on + be + out or on + but. Cognate with Old Frisian abûta (“outside; except”).

more.definition: In, near, or in the general vicinity of (a particular place).; Attending (an educational institution).; Working for (a company) or in (a place or situation).
more.etymology: From Middle English at, from Old English æt (“at, near, by, toward”), from Proto-West Germanic *at, from Proto-Germanic *at (“at, near, to”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éd (“near, at”).

more.definition: At the present time.; Used to introduce a point, a qualification of what has previously been said, a remonstration or a rebuke.; Differently from the immediate past; differently from a more remote past or a possible future; differently from all other times.

more.definition: In good health.; Highly satisfactory; Good, content.

more.definition: Accurately, competently, satisfactorily.; Completely, fully.; To a significant degree.

Cognate with North Frisian hör, Saterland Frisian hier, hiere (“her”), West Frisian har (“her”), Dutch haar (“her”), German Low German hör (“her”), German ihr (“her”).

senses.gloss_en: how (not the general meaning of "in which way", but meaning "from which source" or "from where" exactly)

more.definition: To what degree or extent.; In what manner; By what means.
more.etymology: From Middle English how, hou, hu, hwu, from Old English hū, from Proto-West Germanic *hwō, from Proto-Germanic *hwō (“through what, how”), from the same root as hwæt (“who, what”).

more.definition: Used to state that something is in a certain way or state.
more.etymology: From Middle English how, hou, hu, hwu, from Old English hū, from Proto-West Germanic *hwō, from Proto-Germanic *hwō (“through what, how”), from the same root as hwæt (“who, what”).

more.etymology: From Middle English willen, wullen, wollen, from Old English willan (“to want”), from Proto-West Germanic *willjan, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”).

senses.gloss_en: to wish, to will, to want, to desire

more.etymology: Old Norse vantabor. From Middle English wanten (“to lack, to need”), from Old Norse vanta (“to lack”), from Proto-Germanic *wanatōną (“to be wanting, lack”), from *wanô (“lack, deficiency”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weh₂- (“empty”). Cognate with Middle High German wan (“not full, empty”), Middle Dutch wan (“empty, poor”), Old English wana (“want, lack, absence, deficiency”), Latin vanus (“empty”). See wan, wan-.

more.definition: Introducing a complete question.; With a negative, used rhetorically to make a suggestion.; Introducing a verb phrase (bare infinitive clause).

more.definition: Used to indicate source or provenance.; Originating at (a year, time, etc.); Used to indicate a starting point or initial reference.

more.definition: At what time? At which time? Upon which occasion or circumstance? more.etymology: From Middle English when(ne), whan(ne), from Old English hwonne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwannē, from Proto-West Germanic *hwan, from Proto-Germanic *hwan (“at what time, when”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís (interrogative base).

more.definition: At (or as soon as) that time that; at the (or any and every) time that; if.; During the time that; at the time of the action of the following clause or participle phrase.; At what time; at which time.

senses.gloss_en: oh, oh no, you don’t, say

more.definition: Used to gain someone's attention before making an inquiry or suggestion
more.etymology: From Middle English saien, sain, san, secgan, segen, seien, sein, seiȝen, sugen, sægen, ziggen, from Old English seċġan, secgean, secggan, secggean, seggan, sæċġan (“to say, speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną (“to say”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-h₁-yé-, a suffixed o-grade form of *sekʷ- (“to say”).

senses.gloss_en: to speak, to talk, to utter, to say

more.definition: To pronounce.; To recite.; To tell, either verbally or in writing.
more.etymology: From Middle English saien, sain, san, secgan, segen, seien, sein, seiȝen, sugen, sægen, ziggen, from Old English seċġan, secgean, secggan, secggean, seggan, sæċġan (“to say, speak”), from Proto-West Germanic *saggjan, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaną (“to say”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷ-h₁-yé-, a suffixed o-grade form of *sekʷ- (“to say”).

senses.gloss_en: An exclamation to get attention; hey

more.definition: An exclamation to get attention.; A protest or reprimand.; An expression of surprise.
more.etymology: From Middle English hey, hei, also without h- in ey, from Old English *hē, ēa (interjection), attested as first element in hēlā, ēalā (“O!, alas!, oh!, lo!”). Cognate with Dutch hé, hei (“hi, hey”), German hei (“hey, wow”), Danish and Swedish hej (“hello, hey”), Faroese hey (“hey, hello”), Old Norse, Icelandic and Norwegian hei (“hey”), Polish hej (“hey, hello”), Romanian hei, Russian эй (ej, “hey”); see heigh.

more.definition: Along a path which runs past someone or something.; In the vicinity, near.; To or at a place, as a residence or place of business.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. From Middle English by, bi, from Old English bī (“by; near; around”), from Proto-West Germanic *bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near; by; around; about”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi.

more.definition: Near or next to.; From one side of something to the other, passing close by; past.; Not later than (the given time); not later than the end of (the given time interval); before.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. From Middle English by, bi, from Old English bī (“by; near; around”), from Proto-West Germanic *bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi (“near; by; around; about”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁epi.

more.definition: To have an absolute requirement for.; To want strongly; to feel that one must have something.; To be obliged or required (to do something).
more.etymology: From Middle English neden, from Old English nēodian.

more.definition: An uncertain or unspecified thing; one thing.; A quality to a moderate degree.; A talent or quality that is difficult to specify.
more.etymology: From Middle English somþyng, some-thing, som thing, sum thinge, sum þinge, from Old English sum þing (literally “some thing”), equivalent to some + thing. Compare Old English āwiht (“something”, literally “some thing, any thing”), Swedish någonting (“something”, literally “some thing, any thing”).

more.definition: Likewise.; Also, in addition marks a statement as equally valid as the preceding one.; To an excessive degree, more than enough indicates that the degree of a quality is more than what is needed or wanted.
more.etymology: From Middle English to (“also, in addition to”), from Old English tō (“furthermore, also, besides”), adverbial use of preposition tō (“to, into”). The sense of "in addition, also" deriving from the original meaning of "apart, separately" (compare Old English prefix tō- (“apart”)). Doublet of to; see there for more.

more.definition: To a greater degree or extent.; Used to form the comparative form of adjectives and adverbs.; In negative constructions: any further, any longer; any more.
more.etymology: From Middle English more, from Old English māra (“more”), from Proto-West Germanic *maiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *maizô (“more”), from Proto-Indo-European *mē- (“many”).

more.definition: A road, a direction, a (physical or conceptual) path from one place to another.; A means to enter or leave a place.; A roughly-defined geographical area.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-der. From Middle English way, wey, from Old English weġ, from Proto-West Germanic *weg, from Proto-Germanic *wegaz, from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-. Doublet of voe and possibly via.

more.definition: From a higher position to a lower one; downwards.; To or towards what is considered the bottom of something, irrespective of whether this is presently physically lower.; At a lower or further place or position along a set path.
more.etymology: From Middle English doun, doune (“down”), from Old English dūne (“down”), aphetic form of adūne (“down, downward”), from earlier ofdūne (“down”, literally “off the hill”), from of (“of, off of”) + dūn (“hill, mount, dune, down”). More at Etymology 2 below.

senses.gloss_en: to let, to allow, to make, to have
to create, to shape, to make
to stop moving and instead stick, or make or become bound (more or less literally or figuratively)
to carry it off, to make

more.definition: To build, construct, produce, or originate.; To write or compose.; To bring about; to effect or produce by means of some action.
more.etymology: From Middle English maken, make, from Old English macian (“to build, make, work”), from Proto-West Germanic *makōn (“to build, make, work”), from *mak (“agreeable, comfortable, fit, suitable”), from Proto-Germanic *makaz (“agreeable, comfortable, fit, suitable”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂ǵ-, *meh₂ḱ- (“to knead”) or *meg- (“to be comfortable, pleasant”). Related to match.

more.definition: To a great extent or degree.; Conforming to fact, reality or rule; true.; Used to firmly establish that nothing else surpasses in some respect.
more.etymology: Classical Latin vērāxder. Old French veraibor. From Middle English verray, from Old French verai (“true”), from Early Medieval Latin vērāgus, from Classical Latin vērāx, derived from vērus, from Proto-Italic *wēros, from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁ros. Distantly cognate with Old English wǣr (“true”).

more.definition: At no time; on no occasion; in no circumstance.; Not at any other time; not on any other occasion; not previously.; Negative particle (used to negate verbs in the simple past tense; also used absolutely).
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-osinflu. Proto-West Germanic *aiwder. From Middle English nevere, navere, nævere, from Old English nǣfre (“never”), equivalent to ne + ever.

more.definition: Alone in a category.; Singularly superior; the best.; Without sibling; without a sibling of the same gender.
more.etymology: From Middle English oonly, only, from Old English ānlīċ, ǣnlīċ (“only; singular; solitary”), from Proto-Germanic *ainalīkaz. Cognate with obsolete Dutch eenlijk, German ähnlich (“similar”), Old Norse álíkr, Swedish enlig (“unified”). By surface analysis, on(e) + -ly. * Regarding the different phonological development of only and one, see the note in one.

more.definition: Without others or anything further; exclusively.; No more than; just.; As recently as.
more.etymology: From Middle English oonly, only, from Old English ānlīċ, ǣnlīċ (“only; singular; solitary”), from Proto-Germanic *ainalīkaz. Cognate with obsolete Dutch eenlijk, German ähnlich (“similar”), Old Norse álíkr, Swedish enlig (“unified”). By surface analysis, on(e) + -ly. * Regarding the different phonological development of only and one, see the note in one.

more.definition: Under the condition that; but.; But, except; but in fact.
more.etymology: From Middle English oonly, only, from Old English ānlīċ, ǣnlīċ (“only; singular; solitary”), from Proto-Germanic *ainalīkaz. Cognate with obsolete Dutch eenlijk, German ähnlich (“similar”), Old Norse álíkr, Swedish enlig (“unified”). By surface analysis, on(e) + -ly. * Regarding the different phonological development of only and one, see the note in one.

more.definition: Placed at the end of a sentence to emphasize that something is trivial, small, undemanding or deserving of belittlement.
more.etymology: From Middle English oonly, only, from Old English ānlīċ, ǣnlīċ (“only; singular; solitary”), from Proto-Germanic *ainalīkaz. Cognate with obsolete Dutch eenlijk, German ähnlich (“similar”), Old Norse álíkr, Swedish enlig (“unified”). By surface analysis, on(e) + -ly. * Regarding the different phonological development of only and one, see the note in one.

more.definition: Persons forming or belonging to a particular group, such as a nation, class, ethnic group, country, family, etc.; A group of persons regarded as being servants, followers, companions or subjects of a ruler or leader.; One's colleagues or employees.
more.etymology: From Middle English puple, peple, peeple, from Anglo-Norman people, from Old French pueple, peuple, pople, from Latin populus (“a people, nation”), from Old Latin populus, from earlier poplus, from even earlier poplos, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”) of unknown origin. Doublet of pueblo. Gradually ousted native English lede and, partially, folk. Originally used with singular verbs (e.g.

senses.gloss_en: over (there); yonder (unspecified locative for something at some distance)

more.definition: From one position or location to another, horizontally or approximately so, or along a route visualised as "across".; Across from one side of something to the other.; So as to pass above.
more.etymology: From Middle English over, from Old English ofer, ofor, ouer, from Proto-West Germanic *obar, from Proto-Germanic *uber (“over”), from Proto-Indo-European *upér (“above; over”).

more.definition: Above; higher than; further up than.; Across, from one side to the other.; Across, so as to pass above.
more.etymology: From Middle English over, from Old English ofer, ofor, ouer, from Proto-West Germanic *obar, from Proto-Germanic *uber (“over”), from Proto-Indo-European *upér (“above; over”).

more.definition: On account, for sake [with of].
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Latin causalbor. Old French causebor. From Middle English bi cause, from bi (“by”) + cause, modelled on Old French par cause.

more.definition: By or for the cause that; on this account that; for the reason that.; As is known, inferred, or determined from the fact that.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Latin causalbor. Old French causebor. From Middle English bi cause, from bi (“by”) + cause, modelled on Old French par cause.

more.definition: Small, not large, limited, particularly; Small, limited in size.; Short, limited in extent.
more.etymology: From Middle English litel, litell, luitel, lutel, lutil, luytel, from Old English lȳtel, lyttel, from Proto-West Germanic *lūtil (“little”), from *lūtan (“to bow down, lout”), from Proto-Germanic *lūtaną (“to bow down, lout”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewd- (“to bend, crouch, duck”), equivalent to lout + -le.

more.definition: Not much; not a large amount.
more.etymology: From Middle English litel, litell, luitel, lutel, lutil, luytel, from Old English lȳtel, lyttel, from Proto-West Germanic *lūtil (“little”), from *lūtan (“to bow down, lout”), from Proto-Germanic *lūtaną (“to bow down, lout”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewd- (“to bend, crouch, duck”), equivalent to lout + -le.

more.definition: To make happy or satisfy; to give pleasure to.; To desire; to will; to be pleased by.
more.etymology: From Middle English plesen, plaisen, borrowed from Old French plaise, conjugated form of plaisir or plaire, from Latin placeō (“to please, to seem good”), from the Proto-Indo-European *pleHk- (“pleasingness, permission”). In this sense, displaced native Old English līcian, whence Modern English like.

more.definition: A deep caring for the existence of another.; A profound and caring affection towards someone.; Affectionate, benevolent concern or care for other people or beings, and for their well-being.
more.etymology: From Middle English love, luve, from Old English lufu, from Proto-West Germanic *lubu, from Proto-Germanic *lubō, from Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ- (“love, care, desire”). The close of a letter sense is presumably a truncation of With love or the like. Eclipsed non-native English amour (“love”), borrowed from Norman amour (“love”).

senses.gloss_en: to be fond of, to love

more.definition: To have a strong affection for (someone or something).; To need, thrive on.; To be strongly inclined towards something; an emphatic form of like.
more.etymology: The verb sense is from Middle English loven, luvien, from Old English lufian (“to love”), from Proto-West Germanic *lubōn (“to love”), derived from the noun.

more.definition: Used to issue an instruction (traditionally seen as carrying less force of authority than alternatives such as 'shall' or 'must').; Used to give advice or opinion that an action is, or would have been, beneficial or desirable.; With verbs such as 'see' or 'hear', usually in the second person, used to point out something remarkable in either a good or bad way.
more.etymology: From Middle English scholde, from Old English sċolde, first and third person preterite form of sċulan (“should,” “have to,” “to owe”), the ancestor of English shall. By surface analysis, shall + -ed. Cognate with German sollte, Gothic 𐍃𐌺𐌿𐌻𐌳𐌰 (skulda), Swedish skulle. Related to Middle English shild and shildy.

senses.gloss_en: to mean, to interpret, to understand

more.definition: To intend, to plan (to do); to have as one's intention.; To have as intentions of a given kind.; To intend (something) for a given purpose or fate; to predestine.
more.etymology: From Middle English menen (“to intend; remember; lament; comfort”), from Old English mǣnan (“to mean, complain”), Proto-West Germanic *mainijan, from Proto-Germanic *mainijaną (“to mean, think; complain”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyn- (“to think”), or perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *meyno-, extended form of Proto-Indo-European *mey-.

more.definition: Of a person, regretful or apologetic for one's actions.; Of a person, grieved or saddened, especially by the loss of something or someone.; Poor, pitifully sad or regrettable.
more.etymology: From Middle English sory, from Old English sāriġ (“feeling or expressing grief, sorry, grieved, sorrowful, sad, mournful, bitter”), from Proto-West Germanic *sairag, from Proto-Germanic *sairagaz (“sad”), from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂yro (“hard, rough, painful”).

more.definition: To transfer one's possession or holding of (something) to (someone).; To make a present or gift of.; To pledge.
more.etymology: From Middle English given, yeven, yiven, ȝiven, from merger of Old English ġefan, ġeofan, ġiefan, ġifan, ġiofan, ġyfan (“to give”) and Old Norse gefa (“to give”), from Proto-Germanic *gebaną (“to give”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰebʰ- (“to give; to take”). Displaced yive, from Middle English yiven, of the same origin, from influence of Old Norse gefa.

more.definition: In a direction away from the speaker or other reference point.; Into a state of non-operation or non-existence.; So as to remove or separate, or be removed or separated.
more.etymology: From Middle English of, from Old English of, af, æf (“from, off, away”), from Proto-West Germanic *ab, from Proto-Germanic *ab (“from”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epo (“from, off, back”). Doublet of of.

more.definition: To express appreciation or gratitude toward (someone or something).; In the future tense in the form one will thank someone to do something, chiefly expressing a command or criticism: to request that (someone) do something.; To respond to (someone) out of, or as if out of, appreciation or gratitude.
more.etymology: From Middle English thanken (“to express gratitude, give thanks; to congratulate, rejoice with, or wish joy to; to extol; to hold responsible for”), from Old English þancian, þoncian (“to thank”), from Proto-West Germanic *þankōn, from Proto-Germanic *þankōną (“to thank”), from *þankaz (see etymology 1) + *-ōną (suffix forming infinitives of verbs from nouns).

more.definition: Any thing(s) or person(s).
more.etymology: From Middle English any, eny, ony, ani, aniȝ, eniȝ, æniȝ, from Old English ǣniġ (“any”), from Proto-West Germanic *ainīg, *ainag, from Proto-Germanic *ainagaz, from Proto-Germanic *ainaz (“one”), equivalent to one + -y.

more.definition: A numerical value equal to 2; the number following one and preceding three.; Describing a set or group with two elements.
more.etymology: PIE word *dwóh₁ From Middle English two, twa, from Old English twā, feminine and neuter of twēġen (whence twain), from Proto-West Germanic *twai-, from Proto-Germanic *twai, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁.

more.definition: Flat and level.; Without great variation.; Equal in proportion, quantity, size, etc.
more.etymology: From Middle English even, from Old English efn (“flat; level, even, equal”), from Proto-West Germanic *ebn, from Proto-Germanic *ebnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)em-no- (“equal, straight; flat, level, even”).

more.definition: In reality (used to imply an extreme example in the case mentioned).; Used to emphasise a comparative.; Used to indicate a further degree of comparison.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *(h₁)ém-no-der. Inherited from Middle English evene, from Old English efne, from efn (“even”) + -e (adverbial suffix).

more.definition: To a great extent.; for emphasis or to indicate a great difference; Often; frequently.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-lósder. From Middle English muche (“much, great”), apocopated variant of muchel (“much, great”), from Old English myċel, miċel (“big, much”), from Proto-West Germanic *mikil, from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz (“great, many, much”), from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“big, stour, great”). See also mickle, muckle.

more.definition: A large amount of.; Used to indicate, demonstrate or compare the quantity of something.; many ( + plural countable noun).
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-lósder. From Middle English muche (“much, great”), apocopated variant of muchel (“much, great”), from Old English myċel, miċel (“big, much”), from Proto-West Germanic *mikil, from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz (“great, many, much”), from Proto-Indo-European *meǵh₂- (“big, stour, great”). See also mickle, muckle.

more.definition: Physically secure and certain, non-failing, reliable.; Certain in one's knowledge or belief.; Certain to act or be a specified way.
more.etymology: From Middle English sure, seur, sur, from Middle French sur or Old French seür, from Latin sēcūrus (“secure”, literally “carefree”), from sē- (“apart”) + cūra (“care”) (compare Old English orsorg (“carefree”), from or- (“without”) + sorg (“care”)). See cure. Doublet of secure and the now obsolete or dialectal sicker (“certain, safe”).

more.definition: That which is considered to exist as a separate entity, object, quality or concept.; A word, symbol, sign, or other referent that can be used to refer to any entity.; An individual object or distinct entity.
more.etymology: From Middle English thing, from Old English þing, from Proto-West Germanic *þing, from Proto-Germanic *þingą.

more.definition: Action given to provide assistance; aid.; Something or someone which provides assistance with a task.; Documentation provided with computer software that could be accessed using the computer.
more.etymology: From Middle English help, from Old English help (“help, aid, assistance, relief”), from Proto-Germanic *helpō (“help”), *hilpiz, *hulpiz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (“to help”).

examples.text: Can you help me, please?

translations.de: Kannst du mir bitte helfen?
translations.fr: Peux-tu m'aider, s'il te plaît ?
translations.pt: Você pode me ajudar, por favor?

examples.text: He helped his sister with the move.

translations.de: Er hat seiner Schwester beim Umzug geholfen.
translations.fr: Il a aidé sa sœur à déménager.
translations.pt: Ele ajudou a irmã com a mudança.

more.definition: To provide assistance to (someone or something).; To assist (a person) in getting something, especially food or drink at table; used with to.; To contribute in some way to.
collocations: help yourself — take what you want
more.etymology: From Middle English helpen, from Old English helpan (“to help, aid, assist, benefit, relieve, cure”), from Proto-West Germanic *helpan, Proto-Germanic *helpaną (“to help”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- (“to help”).

more.definition: Preceding all others of a series or kind; the ordinal of one; earliest.; Most eminent or exalted; most excellent; chief; highest.; Of or belonging to a first family.
more.etymology: From Middle English first, furst, ferst, fyrst, from Old English fyrest, from Proto-West Germanic *furist, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz (“first, foremost”), superlative of Proto-Germanic *furai, *furi (“before”), from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”), from *per- (“before; first”), equivalent to fore + -est.

more.definition: Before anything else; firstly.; For the first time.
more.etymology: From Middle English first, furst, ferst, fyrst, from Old English fyrest, from Proto-West Germanic *furist, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz (“first, foremost”), superlative of Proto-Germanic *furai, *furi (“before”), from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”), from *per- (“before; first”), equivalent to fore + -est.

more.definition: To or towards the inside of.; To or towards the region of.; To the condition or state.
more.etymology: From Middle English in-to, from Old English intō, equivalent to in + to. Cognate with Scots intae.

more.definition: Any object, act, state, event, or fact whatsoever; a thing of any kind; something or other.; Expressing an indefinite comparison.
more.etymology: From Middle English anything, enything, onything, from Late Old English aniþing, from earlier ǣniġ þing (literally “any thing”), equivalent to any + thing.

more.definition: Not moving; calm.; Not effervescing; not sparkling.; Uttering no sound; silent.
more.etymology: From Middle English stille (“motionless, stationary”), from Old English stille (“still, quiet”), from Proto-West Germanic *stillī, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)telH- (“to be silent; to be still”).

more.definition: Without motion.; Up to a time, as in the preceding time.; To an even greater degree. Used to modify comparative adjectives or adverbs.
more.etymology: From Middle English stille (“motionless, stationary”), from Old English stille (“still, quiet”), from Proto-West Germanic *stillī, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)telH- (“to be silent; to be still”).

senses.gloss_en: to find, to consider, to deem

more.definition: To encounter or discover by accident; to happen upon.; To encounter or discover something being searched for; to locate.; To locate on behalf of another.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *pent-der. Inherited from Middle English fynden, from Old English findan, from Proto-West Germanic *finþan, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną, a secondary verb from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass; path bridge”).

more.definition: The state of organisms preceding their death, characterized by biological processes such as metabolism and reproduction and distinguishing them from inanimate objects; the state of being alive and living.; The status possessed by any of a number of entities, including animals, plants, fungi, bacteria, and sometimes viruses, which have the properties of replication and metabolism.; The animating principle or force that keeps an inorganic thing or concept metaphorically alive (dynamic, relevant, etc) and makes it a "living document", "living constitution", etc.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *leyp-der. Proto-Germanic *lībanąder. From Middle English lyf, from Old English līf, from Proto-West Germanic *līb, from Proto-Germanic *lībą (“life, body”), from *lībaną (“to remain, stay, be left”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick, glue”).

more.definition: Not any thing; no thing.; An absence of anything, including empty space, brightness, darkness, matter, or a vacuum.
more.etymology: From Middle English nothyng, noon thing, non thing, na þing, nan thing, nan þing, from Old English nāþing, nān þing (“nothing”, literally “not any thing”), equivalent to no + thing. Compare Old English nāwiht (“nothing”, literally “no thing”), Swedish ingenting (“nothing”, literally “not any thing, no thing”).

more.definition: A man of a higher rank or position.; A respectful term of address to a man of higher rank or position, particularly; to a knight or other low member of the peerage.
more.etymology: From Middle English sir, unstressed form of sire, borrowed from Old French sire (“master, sir, lord”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”), from senex (“old”). Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, senior, señor, senyor, signore, and sire.

more.definition: The time when the Sun is above the horizon and it lights the sky.; A period of time equal or almost equal to a full day-night cycle, being 24 hours long.; The time taken for the Sun to seem to be in the same place in the sky twice; a solar day.
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle English day, from Old English dæġ, from Proto-West Germanic *dag, from Proto-Germanic *dagaz (“day”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn”).

more.definition: A being such as a monotheistic God: a single divine creator and ruler of the universe.
more.etymology: Derived from Middle English God. From a proprialization of the common noun, god.

more.definition: A deity or supreme being; a supernatural, typically immortal, being with superior powers, to which personhood is attributed.; A representation of a deity, especially a statue or statuette.; Something or someone particularly revered, worshipped, idealized, admired and/or followed.
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle English god, from Old English god, originally neuter, then changed to masculine to reflect the change in religion to Christianity, from Proto-West Germanic *god n, from Proto-Germanic *gudą; see there for further origin.

more.definition: Labour, occupation, job.; The place where one is employed.; One's employer.
more.etymology: From Middle English work, werk, from Old English weorc, from Proto-West Germanic *werk, from Proto-Germanic *werką (“work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom (“work”), from Proto-Indo-European *werǵ- (“to make”).

senses.gloss_en: to function, to work, to operate, to perform

more.definition: To do a specific task by employing physical or mental powers.; Said of one's workplace (building), or one's department, or one's trade (sphere of business) [with in or at].; Said of one's job title [with as].
more.etymology: From Middle English werken and worchen, from Old English wyrċan and wircan (Mercian), from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną (“to work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥ǵyéti (“to be working, to be at work”), from the root *werǵ-.

more.definition: Belonging to, from, of, or relating to, them (plural).; Belonging to someone (one person, singular), or occasionally to something.
more.etymology: Old Norse þeirader. From Old Norse þeira, þeirra. Replaced native Old English heora.

senses.gloss_en: Um; uh (space filler or pause during conversation).

more.definition: Expression of thought, confusion, or uncertainty.; Expression of discomfort or reservation; a hesitation preceding awkward information or innuendo.; Space filler or pause during conversation.
more.etymology: Onomatopoeia of the natural expression of thought. Compare with er.

more.definition: Another time: indicating a repeat of an action.; Back (to a former place or state).; Over and above a factor of one.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ-der. From Middle English agayn, from Old English onġēan (“against, again”), from Proto-West Germanic *in gagin, from Proto-Germanic *in gagin. Cognate with German entgegen (“contrary to”), North Frisian ijen (“against”), Danish igen (“again”), Swedish igen (“again”), and Norwegian Bokmål igjen (“again”), and Icelandic í gegnum (“through”). By surface analysis, on- + gain (“against”).

more.definition: Perhaps, possibly.; Perhaps that is true (expressing no commitment to a decision or a neutral viewpoint to a statement).; Certainly.
more.etymology: From an ellipsis of Middle English it may be, equivalent to may + be. Compare mayhap.

more.definition: To do as a requirement; indicates that the sentence subject is required as an imperative or directive to execute the sentence predicate, with failure to do so resulting in a failure or negative consequence.; To do with certainty; indicates that the speaker is certain that the subject will have executed the predicate.; Used to indicate that something is very likely, probable, or certain to be true.
more.etymology: From Middle English moste ("must", literally, "had to", the past tense of Middle English moten (“to have to”)), from Old English mōste (“had to”), 1st & 3rd person singular past tense of mōtan (“to be allowed, be able to, have the opportunity to, be compelled to, must, may”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtaną. Cognate with Dutch moest (“had to”), German musste (“had to”), Swedish måste (“must, have to, be obliged to”).

more.definition: At an earlier time.; In advance in position or sequence; ahead.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Proto-Germanic *bider. Inherited from Middle English before /bifore, from Old English beforan, from be- + foran (“before”), from fore, from Proto-Germanic *furai, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“front”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian befoar (“before”), German Low German bevör (“before”), German bevor (“before”).

more.definition: In advance of the time when.; Rather or sooner than.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Proto-Germanic *bider. Inherited from Middle English before /bifore, from Old English beforan, from be- + foran (“before”), from fore, from Proto-Germanic *furai, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“front”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian befoar (“before”), German Low German bevör (“before”), German bevor (“before”).

more.definition: Earlier than (in time).; In front of in space.; In the presence of.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Proto-Germanic *bider. Inherited from Middle English before /bifore, from Old English beforan, from be- + foran (“before”), from fore, from Proto-Germanic *furai, from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“front”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian befoar (“before”), German Low German bevör (“before”), German bevor (“before”).

From Middle English other, from Old English ōþer (“other, second”), from Proto-West Germanic *ą̄þar, *anþar, from Proto-Germanic *anþeraz (“other, second”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énteros (“other”).

examples.text: I am waiting for the bus.

translations.de: Ich warte auf den Bus.
translations.fr: J'attends le bus.
translations.pt: Estou esperando o ônibus.

examples.text: We waited an hour for you.

translations.de: Wir haben eine Stunde auf dich gewartet.
translations.fr: Nous t'avons attendu pendant une heure.
translations.pt: Esperamos uma hora por você.

more.definition: To delay movement or action until some event or time; to remain neglected or in readiness.; To wait tables; to serve customers in a restaurant or other eating establishment.; To remain faithful to one’s partner or betrothed during a prolonged period of absence.
collocations: wait a minute — just a moment
more.etymology: From Middle English waiten, from Anglo-Norman waiter, waitier (compare French guetter from Old French gaitier, guaitier), from Frankish *wahtwēn (“to watch, guard”), derivative of Frankish *wahtu (“guard, watch”), from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō (“guard, watch”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be fresh, cheerful, awake”).

senses.gloss_en: to stop, to quit, to give up
to cease, to stop, to quit

more.definition: To cease moving.; Not to continue.; To cause (something) to cease moving or progressing.
more.etymology: From Middle English stoppen, stoppien, from Old English stoppian (“to stop, close”), from Proto-West Germanic *stoppōn, from Proto-Germanic *stuppōną (“to stop, close”), *stuppijaną (“to push, pierce, prick”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-, *(s)tewb- (“to push; stick”), from *(s)tew- (“to bump; impact; butt; push; beat; strike; hit”).

more.definition: A cry or shout.; The characteristic cry of a bird or other animal.; A beckoning or summoning.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *gels-der. Proto-Germanic *kalzazder. Old English cealliander. From Middle English callen, from Old English ċeallian (“to call, shout”) and Old Norse kalla (“to call; shout; refer to as; name”); both from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną (“to call, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *golH-so- (“voice, cry”), from *gel(H)- (“to vocalize, call, shout”). * Albanian gjuhë (“language, tongue”).

more.definition: To request, summon, or beckon.; To cry or shout.; To utter in a loud or distinct voice.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *gels-der. Proto-Germanic *kalzazder. Old English cealliander. From Middle English callen, from Old English ċeallian (“to call, shout”) and Old Norse kalla (“to call; shout; refer to as; name”); both from Proto-Germanic *kalzōną (“to call, shout”), from Proto-Indo-European *golH-so- (“voice, cry”), from *gel(H)- (“to vocalize, call, shout”). * Albanian gjuhë (“language, tongue”).

more.definition: Signifies that the action of the clause it starts takes place before the action of the other clause.
more.etymology: From Middle English after, from Old English æfter, from Proto-West Germanic *aftar, from Proto-Germanic *after, *aftiri, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epoteros (“further behind, further away”), from *h₂epo (“off, away”).

more.definition: Subsequently to; following in time; later than.; Subsequently to and as a result of.; Subsequently to and considering.
more.etymology: From Middle English after, from Old English æfter, from Proto-West Germanic *aftar, from Proto-Germanic *after, *aftiri, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epoteros (“further behind, further away”), from *h₂epo (“off, away”).

more.definition: A conversation or discussion; usually serious, but informal.; A lecture.; Gossip; rumour.
more.etymology: From Middle English talk, talke (“conversation; discourse”), from the verb (see above).

senses.gloss_en: to speak, to talk, to utter, to say
to speak, to propose, to talk

more.definition: To communicate, usually by means of speech.; To discuss; to talk about.; To speak (a certain language).
more.etymology: From Middle English talken, talkien, from Old English *tealcian (“to talk, chat”), from Proto-West Germanic *talkōn, from Proto-Germanic *talkōną (“to talk, chatter”), frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *talōną (“to count, recount, tell”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol-, *del- (“to aim, calculate, adjust, count”), equivalent to tell + -k. Cognates Cognate with Low German taalken (“to chatter, gossip, talk”).

more.definition: From a place, hence.; Aside; off; in another direction.; Aside, so as to discard something.
more.etymology: From Middle English away, awey, awei, oway, o wey, on way, from Old English āweġ, onweġ (“away”), originally on weġ (“on one's way; onward; on”), equivalent to a- (“on”) + way. Cognate with Scots awa, away (“away”), Old Frisian aweg, awei (“away”), Saterland Frisian wäch, wääge (“away”), Dutch weg (“away”), German weg (“away”), Danish væk (“away”), Swedish i väg (“away; off; along”).

more.definition: At that time; then.
more.etymology: From Middle English than, thanne (“than; then”), from Old English þanne, a variant of þonne (“then; when; than”), from Proto-West Germanic *þannē, an alteration of *þan (“then; than”), from Proto-Germanic *þan (“then; than”), from earlier *þam, from Proto-Indo-European *tóm, accusative masculine of *só (“that”, demonstrative pronoun).

more.definition: Used in comparisons, to introduce the basis of comparison.
more.etymology: From Middle English than, thanne (“than; then”), from Old English þanne, a variant of þonne (“then; when; than”), from Proto-West Germanic *þannē, an alteration of *þan (“then; than”), from Proto-Germanic *þan (“then; than”), from earlier *þam, from Proto-Indo-European *tóm, accusative masculine of *só (“that”, demonstrative pronoun).

more.definition: A representation created in the mind without the use of one's faculties of vision, sound, smell, touch, or taste; an instance of thinking.; The operation by which mental activity arise or are manipulated; the process of thinking; the agency by which thinking is accomplished.; A way of thinking (associated with a group, nation, region or idea).
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *teng-der. From Middle English thought, ithoȝt, from Old English þōht, ġeþōht, from Proto-West Germanic *þą̄ht, from Proto-Germanic *þanhtaz, *gaþanhtą (“thought”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think”).

more.definition: One’s own dwelling place; the house or structure in which one lives; especially the house in which one lives with one's family; the habitual abode of one’s family.; The place (residence, settlement, country, etc.), where a person was born or raised; a childhood or parental home; the home of one’s parents or guardian.; The abiding place of the affections, especially of the domestic affections.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *tḱéytibf. From Middle English hom, from Old English hām, from Proto-West Germanic *haim, from Proto-Germanic *haimaz (“home, village”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos (“village, home”), from the root *tḱey-. Doublet of heyem.

more.definition: The time when the Sun is below the horizon when the sky is dark.; The period of darkness beginning at the end of evening astronomical twilight when the sun is 18 degrees below the horizon, and ending at the beginning of morning astronomical twilight.; A period of time often defined in the legal system as beginning 30 minutes after sunset, and ending 30 minutes before sunrise.
more.etymology: From Middle English nighte, night, nyght, niȝt, naht, from Old English niht, from Proto-West Germanic *naht (“night”), from Proto-Germanic *nahts (“night”), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts (“night”).

senses.gloss_en: to put, to add, to pour
to place, to put, to stand

more.definition: To physically place (something or somebody, in, at, around, etc. someplace); To place in abstract; to attach or attribute; to assign.; To bring or set (into a certain relation, state or condition).
more.etymology: From Middle English putten, pitten, pytten, puten, poten, from Old English putian, *pūtian ("to push, put out"; attested by derivative putung (“pushing, impulse, instigation, urging”)) and potian (“to push, thrust, strike, butt, goad”), both from Proto-West Germanic *putōn, from Proto-Germanic *putōną (“to stick, stab”), which is of uncertain origin.

more.definition: Taking up a lot of space; large.; Much, more than usual.; Intensifying a word or expression, used in mild oaths.
more.etymology: From Middle English greet, grete (“great, large”), from Old English grēat (“big, massive; tall; thick; coarse”), from Proto-West Germanic *graut, from Proto-Germanic *grautaz (“coarse, crude; big, large”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrewd-, *gʰer- (“to rub; to stroke; to grind; to remove”).

more.definition: Final, ultimate, coming after all others of its kind.; Most recent, latest, last so far.; Farthest of all from a given quality, character, or condition; most unlikely, or least preferable.
more.etymology: From Middle English laste, latst, syncopated variant of latest, both ultimately from Old English latost. Doublet of latest.

more.definition: To endure, continue over time.; To hold out, continue undefeated or entire.; To purposefully refrain from orgasm
more.etymology: From Middle English lasten, from Old English lǣstan, from Proto-West Germanic *laistijan, from Proto-Germanic *laistijaną. Cognate with German leisten (“yield”).

more.definition: All the things under discussion.; Many or most things.; A state of well-being (from all parts of the whole).
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle English every thing; univerbation of every + thing.

more.definition: Recently made, or created.; Of recent origin; having taken place recently.; Additional; recently discovered.
more.etymology: From Middle English neowe, neue, new, newe, nywe, from Old English nēowe, nīewe, nīowe, nīwe, from Proto-West Germanic *niwi, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz (“new”), from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, *néwyos (“new”). Compare also Old English nū (“now”). More at now. Doublet of nuevo, novuss, and neo-.

more.definition: At all times; throughout all time; since the beginning.; Constantly during a certain period, or regularly at stated intervals (opposed to sometimes or occasionally).; if necessary, or if there is no better option; in any event.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ-der. From Middle English alweyes, alwayes, alweys, a variant of Middle English alwey, alway (“always”), from Old English ealneġ, ealne weġ (“always, perpetually”, literally “all the way, all the while, continuously”), from ealne + weġ (accusative case), equivalent to alway + -s. Cognate with Scots always (“always”), Low German allerwegens (“very often”, literally “all ways'”).

more.definition: To continue in (a course or mode of action); to not intermit or fall from; to uphold or maintain.; To remain faithful to a given promise or word.; To maintain possession of.
more.etymology: From Middle English kepen (“to keep, guard, look after, watch”), from Old English cēpan (“to seize, hold, observe”), from Proto-West Germanic *kōpijan, from Proto-Germanic *kōpijaną (“to look, heed, watch, observe”) (compare West Frisian kypje (“to look”)), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵab-, *ǵāb- (“to look after”) (compare Lithuanian žẽbti (“to eat reluctantly”), Russian забо́та (zabóta, “care, worry”)).

more.definition: Having much distance in space from one end to the other.; Specifically, having much distance in a horizontal dimension (see also Usage Notes below).; Travelling a great distance.
more.etymology: From Middle English long, lang, from Old English long, lang (“long, tall, lasting”), from Proto-West Germanic *lang, from Proto-Germanic *langaz (“long”), from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos (“long”).

senses.gloss_en: to abandon, to leave, to quit, to forsake

more.definition: To cause or allow (something) to remain as available; to refrain from taking (something) away; to stop short of consuming or otherwise depleting (something) entirely.; To cause, to result in.; To put; to place; to deposit; to deliver, with a sense of withdrawing oneself.
more.etymology: From Middle English leven, from Old English lǣfan (“to leave”), from Proto-West Germanic *laibijan, from Proto-Germanic *laibijaną (“to let stay, leave”), causative of *lībaną (“to stay, remain”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to stick; fat”).

more.definition: A generally accepted means of exchange.; A currency maintained by a state or other entity which can guarantee its value (such as a monetary union).; Hard cash in the form of banknotes and coins, as opposed to cheques, credit cards, or credit more generally.
more.etymology: Anglo-Norman muneiebor. From Middle English moneye, moneie, money, borrowed from Anglo-Norman muneie (“money”), from Latin monēta (“money, a place for coining money, coin, mint”), from the name of the temple of Juno Moneta in Rome, where a mint was. In this sense, displaced native Old English feoh, whence English fee.

more.definition: So as to form a circle or trace a circular path, or approximation thereof.; So as to surround or be near.; Nearly; approximately; about.
more.etymology: From Middle English around, arounde, from a- (from Old English a- (“on, at”)) + Middle English round (“circle, round”) borrowed from French, equivalent to a- + round. Cognate with Scots aroond, aroon (“around”). Displaced earlier Middle English umbe, embe (“around”) (from Old English ymbe (“around”)).

more.definition: Forming a circle or closed curve containing (something).; Centred upon; surrounding; regarding.; Following the perimeter of a specified area and returning to the starting point.
more.etymology: From Middle English around, arounde, from a- (from Old English a- (“on, at”)) + Middle English round (“circle, round”) borrowed from French, equivalent to a- + round. Cognate with Scots aroond, aroon (“around”). Displaced earlier Middle English umbe, embe (“around”) (from Old English ymbe (“around”)).

more.definition: Any nounal word or phrase which indicates a particular person, place, class, or thing.; A reputation.; An abusive or insulting epithet.
more.etymology: PIE word *h₁nómn̥ Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ Proto-Germanic *namô Proto-West Germanic *namō Old English nama Middle English name English name From Middle English name, nome, from Old English nama, noma, from Proto-West Germanic *namō, from Proto-Germanic *namô (“name”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ (“name”).

more.definition: To give a name to.; To mention, specify.; To identify as relevant or important
more.etymology: From Middle English namen, from Old English namian (“to name, mention”) and ġenamian (“to name, call, appoint”), from Proto-West Germanic *namōn (“to name”). Cognate with West Frisian neame (“to name; to mention”). Compare also Old English nemnan, nemnian (“to name, give a name to a person or thing”).

more.definition: An open space, particularly a city square, market square, or courtyard.; A street, sometimes but not always surrounding a public place, square, or plaza of the same name.; An inhabited area: a village, town, or city.
more.etymology: From Middle English place, conflation of Old English plæċe (“place, an open space, street”) and Old French place (“place, an open space”), both from Latin platēa (“plaza, wide street”), from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), shortening of πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂- (“to spread”), extended form of *pleh₂- (“flat”).

senses.gloss_en: to place, to put, to stand

more.definition: To put (someone or something) in a specific location.; To earn a given spot in a competition; to rank at a certain position ((often followed by an ordinal)).; To finish second, especially of horses or dogs.
more.etymology: From Middle English placen, from the noun (see above).

more.definition: Continuously, constantly, all the time (for the complete duration).; At any time.; As intensifier following an interrogative word.
more.etymology: From Middle English ever, from Old English ǣfre, originally a phrase whose first element undoubtedly consists of Old English ā (“ever, always”) + in (“in”) + an element possibly from feorh (“life, existence”) (dative fēore). Compare Old English ā tō fēore (“ever in life”), Old English feorhlīf (“life”) from feorh (“life”) + līf (“life”).

more.definition: To become aware of through the skin; to use the sense of touch on.; To find one's way (literally or figuratively) by touching or using cautious movements.; To receive information by touch or by any neurons other than those responsible for sight, smell, taste, or hearing.
more.etymology: From Middle English felen, from Old English fēlan, from Proto-West Germanic *fōlijan. Cognate with Dutch voelen and German fühlen.

more.definition: A male parent, especially of a human; a male who parents a child (which he has sired, adopted, fostered, etc.).; A male ancestor more remote than a parent; a progenitor; especially, a first ancestor.; A term of respectful address for an elderly man.
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle English fader, from Old English fæder, from Proto-West Germanic *fader, from Proto-Germanic *fadēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr, possibly from *peh₂- + *-tḗr. Doublet of ayr, faeder, athair, padre, pater, and père.

more.definition: An effigy of a man burned on a bonfire on the anniversary of the Gunpowder Plot (5th November).; A man or boy; a fellow.; A person (see usage notes).
more.etymology: Coined by semantic widening from the name of Guy Fawkes (1570–1606), an English Catholic executed for his role in the Gunpowder Plot, which also came to refer to effigies of his image burned annually on Guy Fawkes Night.

more.definition: Of an object, concept, relationship, etc., having existed for a relatively long period of time.; Of a living being, having lived for most of the expected years.; Of a perishable item, having existed for most of, or more than, its shelf life.
more.etymology: Inherited from Middle English old, oold, from Old English ald, eald (“old, aged, ancient, antique, primeval”), from Proto-West Germanic *ald, from Proto-Germanic *aldaz (“grown-up”), originally a participle form, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eltós (“grown, tall, big”).

more.definition: What one or ones (of those mentioned or implied).; The/Any ones that; whichever.; Referring to a preceding noun.
more.etymology: From Middle English which, hwic, wilche, hwilch, whilk, hwilc, from Old English hwelċ (“which”), from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz (“what kind”, literally “like what”), derived from *hwaz.

examples.text: They live in a big city.

translations.de: Sie wohnen in einer großen Stadt.
translations.fr: Ils habitent dans une grande ville.
translations.pt: Eles moram em uma cidade grande.

examples.text: This shirt is too big for me.

translations.de: Dieses Hemd ist mir zu groß.
translations.fr: Cette chemise est trop grande pour moi.
translations.pt: Esta camisa é grande demais para mim.

more.definition: Of great size, large.; Fat.; Large with young; pregnant; swelling; ready to give birth or produce.
collocations: big deal — something important (often ironic)
more.etymology: Inherited from Northern Middle English big, bigge (“powerful, strong”), possibly from a dialect of Old Norse. Ultimately perhaps a derivative of Proto-Germanic *bugja- (“swollen up, thick”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew-, *bu- (“to swell”), in which case big would be related to bogey, bugbear, and bug. Compare dialectal Norwegian bugge (“great man”), Low German Bögge, Boggelmann.

more.definition: A large quantity or number; a great deal.; A separate, appropriated portion; a quantized, subdivided set consisting a whole.; One or more items auctioned or sold as a unit, separate from other items.
more.etymology: From Middle English lot, from Old English hlot (“portion, choice, decision”), from Proto-West Germanic *hlut, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą. Cognate with North Frisian lod, Saterland Frisian Lot, West Frisian lot, Dutch lot, French lot, German Low German Lott, Middle High German luz. Doublet of lotto. Related also to German Los.

more.definition: Having completed or finished an activity.; Completed or finished.; Ready, fully cooked.
more.etymology: From Middle English don, idon, ydon, ȝedon, gedon, from Old English dōn, ġedōn, from Proto-West Germanic *dān, from Proto-Germanic *dēnaz (past participle of *dōną (“to do”)). Equivalent to do + -en (past participle ending). Cognate with Scots dune, deen, dene, dane (“done”), Saterland Frisian däin (“done”), West Frisian dien (“done”), Dutch gedaan (“done”), German Low German daan (“done”), German getan (“done”).

more.definition: A greeting (salutation) said when meeting someone or acknowledging someone’s arrival or presence.; A greeting used when answering the telephone.; A call for response if it is not clear if anyone is present or listening, or if a telephone conversation may have been disconnected.
more.etymology: First attested in 1826. From holla, hollo (attested 1588). This variant of hallo is often credited to Thomas Edison as a coinage for telephone use, but its appearance in print predates the invention of the telephone by several decades. Ultimately from a variant of Old English ēalā, such as hēlā, which was used colloquially at the time similarly to how hey and (in some dialects) hi are used nowadays.

more.definition: Pleasant, satisfactory, complimentary.; Of a person: friendly, attractive.; Respectable; virtuous.
more.etymology: From Middle English nyce, nice, nys, from Old French nice, niche, nisce (“simple, foolish, ignorant”), from Latin nescius (“ignorant, not knowing”); compare nesciō (“to know not, be ignorant of”), from ne (“not”) + sciō (“to know”).

more.definition: To accept as true, particularly without absolute certainty (i.e., as opposed to knowing).; To accept that someone is telling the truth.; To have been convinced by rational means to accept the truth of a proposition.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *h₁ep-der. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épsder. Proto-Indo-European *h₁épider. Proto-Germanic *bider. Proto-Indo-European *lewbʰ-der. From Middle English beleven, bileven, from Old English belīefan (“to believe”), from Proto-West Germanic *bilaubijan (“to believe”), equivalent to be- + leave (“to give leave or permission to, permit, allow, grant”).

more.definition: A female child.; A woman, especially a young and often attractive woman.; A term of address to a female (see usage notes)
more.etymology: From Middle English gerle, girle, gyrle (“young person (boy or girl)”), perhaps from Old English *gyrele, from Proto-West Germanic *gurilā, from a zero-grade diminutive of *gaurā (“young child”) + *-ilā. Ultimately of unknown origin. Doublet of gal/gyal and gyaru. Cognates Cognate with Yola gurl (“child, girl”), German Gör, Göre (“brat, cheeky young child”), Low German Gör (“child”).

more.definition: One or some person of unspecified or indefinite identity.
more.etymology: From Middle English sum on, sum one, sum oon, equivalent to some + one.

more.definition: Used to express appreciation or gratitude.
more.etymology: From Middle English thanks, thankes, from Old English þancas (“thanks”), from Proto-Germanic *þankōs, nominative plural of *þankaz (“thought, gratitude”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think, feel”). More at thank.

more.definition: An expression of appreciation or gratitude.; Grateful feelings or thoughts; favour, goodwill, graciousness.
more.etymology: From Middle English thanks, thankes, from Old English þancas (“thanks”), from Proto-Germanic *þankōs, nominative plural of *þankaz (“thought, gratitude”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think, feel”). More at thank.

more.definition: A type, race or category; a group of entities that have common characteristics such that they may be grouped together.; A makeshift or otherwise atypical specimen.; Goods or services used as payment, as e.g. in barter.
more.etymology: From Middle English kynde, kinde, from Old English cynd, ġecynd (“inherent nature, disposition, kind, gender, generation, race”), from Proto-West Germanic *kundi, from Proto-Germanic *kinþiz, related to Proto-Germanic *kunją (“race, kin”) and Old English cennan (“to bear, give birth”). Cognate with Old High German gikunt (“nature, kind”), Icelandic kind (“race, species, kind”). Doublet of gens, genesis, and jati.

regional_variants.note: British English says "garden" where American says "yard".

examples.text: The house has a big yard.

translations.de: Das Haus hat einen großen Garten.
translations.fr: La maison a un grand jardin.
translations.pt: A casa tem um jardim grande.

examples.text: There are many old houses on this street.

translations.de: In dieser Straße stehen viele alte Häuser.
translations.fr: Il y a beaucoup de vieilles maisons dans cette rue.
translations.pt: Há muitas casas antigas nesta rua.

more.definition: A structure built or serving as an abode of human beings.; An apartment building within a public housing estate.; A container; a thing which houses another.
collocations: on the house — free, paid by the owner
more.etymology: From Middle English hous, hus, from Old English hūs (“dwelling, shelter, house”), from Proto-West Germanic *hūs, from Proto-Germanic *hūsą (“house”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kews-, from *(s)kewH- (“to cover, hide”). More at hose. Eclipsed non-native Middle English mees, meson, measoun (“house”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman mes, mies, meis, maisun (“house”).

usage_note: The plural is spelled regularly but the s is voiced: /ˈhaʊzɪz/.

more.definition: All of a countable group (considered individually), without exception.; Denotes equal spacing at a stated interval, or a proportion corresponding to such a spacing.; Denotes an abundance of something.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *-osinflu. Proto-West Germanic *aiwder. Inherited from Middle English every, everich, everych, from Old English ǣfre ǣlċ, ǣfre ǣġhwelċ. By surface analysis, ever + each or ever + which.

more.definition: So as to enter (something), pass within or across, and then leave.; So as to progress within (something) or towards the end or limit of (something).; From one side of (an opening) to the other.
more.etymology: From Middle English thurgh, thrugh, thruch, thruh, metathetic variants of thurgh, thurh, from Old English þurh, from Proto-Germanic *þurhw (“through”), from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥h₂kʷe, suffixed zero-grade from *terh₂- (“to pass through”) + *-kʷe (“and”).

more.definition: Ellipsis of of course.
A sequence of events.; A normal or customary sequence.; A programme, a chosen manner of proceeding.
more.etymology: Old French coursbor. From Middle English cours, from Old French cours, from Latin cursus (“course of a race”), from currō (“run”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ḱers- (“to run”). Doublet of cursus and cour.

more.definition: To remain in a particular place, especially for a definite or short period of time; sojourn; abide.; To continue to have a particular quality.; To prop; support; sustain; hold up; steady.
more.etymology: From Middle English steyen, staien, from Old French estayer, estaier (“to fix, prop up, support, stay”), from estaye, estaie (“a prop, stay”), from Middle Dutch staeye (“a prop, stay”), a contracted form of staede, stade (“a prop, stay, help, aid”) (compare Middle Dutch staeyen, staeden (“to make firm, stay, support, hold still, stabilise”)), from Proto-West Germanic *stadi (“a site, place, location, standing”), …

more.definition: On the left side.; Towards the left side.; Towards the political left.
more.etymology: From Middle English left, luft, leoft, lift, lyft, from Old English left, lyft (“weak, clumsy, foolish”), attested in Old English lyftādl (“palsy, paralysis”), from Proto-Germanic *luft-, from *lubjaną (“to castrate, lop off”) (compare dialectal English lib, West Frisian lobje, Dutch lubben), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)lewp-, *(s)lup- (“hanging limply”).

more.definition: A father, a male parent.; Used to address one's father; often capitalized.; Used to address an older adult male.
more.etymology: From Early Modern English dadd, dadde (circa 1500), undoubtedly older, from unrecorded Middle English *dadde, of uncertain ultimate origin. Compare West Frisian deite (“dad, daddy”), Swabian Dede (“Godfather”).

more.definition: A sufficient or adequate number, amount, etc.
more.etymology: From Middle English ynogh, from Old English ġenōg (“enough”), from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz (“enough”) (compare Scots eneuch, West Frisian genôch, Dutch genoeg, German genug, Low German (ge)noog, Danish nok, Swedish nog, Icelandic nógur), from *ganuganą 'to suffice' (compare Old English ġeneah), or from *ga- + an unattested *nōgaz, probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₂nó(n)ḱe (“he has reached, …

more.definition: To be able to go.; To have permission to, be allowed. Used in granting permission and in questions to make polite requests.; Expressing a present possibility; possibly.
more.etymology: From Middle English magen, mauen, mawe, mawen, mayen, maȝen, mouin, mow, mowen, moȝen, mugen, from Old English magan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”), from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe (“to be able”), from *megʰ- (“to be able”).

more.definition: A female parent, especially of a human; a female who parents a child (which she has given birth to, adopted, fostered, etc).; A pregnant female; mother-to-be; a female who gestates a baby.; A female who donates a fertilized egg or donates a body cell which has resulted in a clone.
more.etymology: From Middle English moder, from Old English mōdor, from Proto-West Germanic *mōder, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr. Doublet of Madeira, mata, mater, matrix, and matter. Some have proposed that the "dregs" sense is from Middle Dutch modder (“filth”), from Proto-Germanic *muþraz (“sediment”), but modder is not known in this meaning.

more.definition: Incorrect or untrue.; Asserting something incorrect or untrue.; Immoral, not good, bad.
more.etymology: Old Norse rangrinflu. Old Norse rangrinflu. From Middle English wrong, from Old English wrang (“wrong, twisted, uneven”), from Old Norse rangr, vrangr (“crooked, wrong”), from Proto-Germanic *wrangaz (“crooked, twisted, turned awry”), from Proto-Indo-European *werḱ-, *wrengʰ- (“to twist, weave, tie together”), from *wer- (“to turn, bend”).

more.definition: Something that is immoral or not good.; An instance of wronging someone (sometimes with possessive to indicate the wrongdoer).; The incorrect or unjust position or opinion.
more.etymology: Old Norse rangrinflu. Old Norse rangrinflu. From Middle English wrong, from Old English wrang (“wrong, twisted, uneven”), from Old Norse rangr, vrangr (“crooked, wrong”), from Proto-Germanic *wrangaz (“crooked, twisted, turned awry”), from Proto-Indo-European *werḱ-, *wrengʰ- (“to twist, weave, tie together”), from *wer- (“to turn, bend”).

more.definition: The subjective human experience, regarded collectively; human collective existence; existence in general; the reality we live in.; The subjective human experience, regarded individually.; A majority of people.
more.etymology: From Middle English world, from Old English weorold (“world”), from Proto-West Germanic *weraldi, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz (“lifetime, human existence, world”, literally “age/era of man”), equivalent to wer (“man”) + eld (“age”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English mounde (“world”), from Old French monde, munde (“world”).

more.definition: Of low quality.; Inaccurate; incorrect; Unfavorable; negative; not good.
more.etymology: From Middle English bad, badde (“wicked, evil, depraved”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps a shortening of Old English bæddel (“hermaphrodite”) (for loss of -el compare Middle English muche from Old English myċel, and Middle English wenche from Old English wenċel), or at least related to it and/or to bǣ̆dan (“to defile”), compare Old High German pad (“hermaphrodite”).

more.definition: Power, strength, force, or influence held by a person or group.; Physical strength or force.; The ability to do something.
more.etymology: From Middle English maught, might, miȝt, myght, from Old English maht, meaht, meht, mieht, miht, mæht (“ability, power; strength; virtue”), from Proto-West Germanic *mahti, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz (“ability, power; force, strength”), from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe (“to be able to, to have power”), from *megʰ- (“to be able”), corresponding to Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”) + *-þiz.

more.definition: A numerical value equal to 3; the number following two and preceding four.; Describing a set or group with three elements.
more.etymology: From Middle English thre, threo, thrie, thri, from Old English þrī, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīʀ, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Doublet of tres and trey. Cognate with German drei, Albanian tre, Armenian երեք (erekʻ), Latin trēs, Latvian trīs, Lithuanian trỹs, Greek τρεῖς (treís), Old Church Slavonic трьѥ (trĭje), and others.

more.definition: On the current day or date.; In the current era; nowadays; these days.; On the day of a recurring cycle or event which is currently happening.
more.etymology: From Middle English today, to-daie, todæig, from Old English tōdæġ, tō dæġe (“today”, literally “on [the/this] day, [this] day forward”), equivalent to to + day. Compare Saterland Frisian däälich (“today”), Dutch vandaag (“today”), Old Saxon hindag (“today”, literally “[this] day forward”), German Low German vandage, vandaag (“today”), Swedish i dag, idag (“today”).

more.definition: To use one's sense of hearing and auditory cognition in an intentional way; to make deliberate use of one's ears; to pay attention to or wait for a specific sound.; To accept advice or obey instruction; to agree or assent.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew-der. From Middle English listenen, listnen, alteration (due to Middle English listen (“to listen, give heed to”)) of Old English hlysnan (“to listen”), from Proto-Germanic *hlusnijaną, *hlusnōną (compare Middle High German lüsenen), from Proto-Germanic *hlusēną (compare Old High German hlosēn), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew- (“to hear”). Cognate with Swedish lyssna (“to listen”).

more.definition: To know the meaning of; to parse or have parsed correctly; to comprehend.; To know the meaning of.; To be thoroughly familiar with; to be able to undertake properly.
more.etymology: From Middle English understanden, from Old English understandan (“to understand”), from Proto-West Germanic *understandan (“to stand between, understand”), from Proto-Germanic *understandaną (“to stand between, understand”), equivalent to Old English under- (“between, inter-”) + standan (“to stand”) (Modern English under- + stand).

more.definition: To perceive sounds through the ear.; To perceive (a sound, or something producing a sound) with the ear, to recognize (something) in an auditory way.; To exercise this faculty intentionally; to listen to.
more.etymology: From Middle English har, heoren, her, here, heren, from Old English hēran, hīeran, hīran, hȳran (“to hear”), from Proto-West Germanic *hauʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *hauzijaną (“to hear”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ḱh₂owsyéti (“to be sharp-eared”), from *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”) + *h₂ows- (“ear”) + *-yéti (denominative suffix).

governs.meaning: a past event: I remember meeting her
not forget to do: remember to call

senses.gloss_en: to keep in mind, to memorize, to remember

examples.text: I remember my first day of school.

translations.de: Ich erinnere mich an meinen ersten Schultag.
translations.fr: Je me souviens de mon premier jour d'école.
translations.pt: Eu me lembro do meu primeiro dia de aula.

examples.text: Do you remember her name?

translations.de: Erinnerst du dich an ihren Namen?
translations.fr: Tu te souviens de son nom ?
translations.pt: Você se lembra do nome dela?

more.definition: To recall from one's memory; to have an image in one's memory.; To memorize; to put something into memory.; To keep in mind; to be mindful of.
collocations: as far as I remember — if my memory is right
more.etymology: From Middle English remembren, from Old French remembrer (“to remember”), from Late Latin rememorari (“to remember again”), from re- + memor (“mindful”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)mer- (“to think about, be mindful, remember”). Cognate with Old English mimorian, mymerian (“to remember, commemorate”), Old English māmorian (“to deliberate, plan out, design”). More at mimmer and mammer.

more.definition: To request (information, or an answer to a question).; To request or enquire of (a person).; To request (an item or service) (see also ask for).
more.etymology: From Middle English asken, axen, from Old English āscian, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eys- (“to wish; request”).

more.definition: Belonging to; possessed; acquired and designated by; proper to; property of; titled to; held in one's name; under/using the name of. Often marks a possessive determiner as reflexive, referring back to the subject of the clause or sentence.; Not shared.
more.etymology: From Middle English oun, owen, from Old English āgen (“own, proper, peculiar”), originally the past participle of āgan; from Proto-West Germanic *aigan (“own”), from Proto-Germanic *aiganaz (“own”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eyḱ- (“to have, possess”). Doublet of eigen-.

more.definition: To have rightful possession of (property, goods or capital); to have legal title to; to acquire a property or asset.; To have recognized political sovereignty over a place, territory, as distinct from the ordinary connotation of property ownership.; To defeat or embarrass; to overwhelm.
more.etymology: A back-formation from owner. Compare Old English āgnian, Dutch eigenen, German eignen, Swedish ägna.

more.definition: Not different or other; not another or others; not different as regards self; selfsame; identical.; Lacking variety from; indistinguishable.; Similar, alike.
more.etymology: From Middle English same, from Old Norse samr (“same”) and/or Old English same, sama (“same”) in the phrase swā same (swā) (“in like manner, in the same way (as)”), both from Proto-Germanic *samaz (“same”), from Proto-Indo-European *somHós (“same”). Doublet of some and -some.

more.definition: The identical thing, ditto.; Something similar, something of the identical type.; It or them, without a connotation of similarity.
more.etymology: From Middle English same, from Old Norse samr (“same”) and/or Old English same, sama (“same”) in the phrase swā same (swā) (“in like manner, in the same way (as)”), both from Proto-Germanic *samaz (“same”), from Proto-Indo-European *somHós (“same”). Doublet of some and -some.

more.definition: A play, dance, or other entertainment.; An exhibition of items.; A broadcast program, especially a light entertainment program.
more.etymology: From Middle English schewe, from the verb (schewen).

senses.gloss_en: to show, to present, to indicate, to demonstrate

more.definition: To display, convey or exhibit; to have something available for others to see; to direct attention to something.; To indicate; to convey facts that lead to a conclusion.; To guide or escort; to show the way.
more.etymology: Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁-der. From Middle English schewen, from Old English scēawian (“to look, look at, exhibit, display”), from Proto-West Germanic *skauwōn, from Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look, see”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to heed, look, feel, take note of”); see haw, gaum, caveat, caution.

more.definition: To put to death; to extinguish the life of.; To render inoperative.; To stop, cease, or render void; to terminate.
more.etymology: From Middle English killen, kyllen, cüllen (“to strike, beat, cut”), of obscure origin.
